item.title: Evaporative Cooling and Secondary Combustion in a Liquid-Hydrocarbon Rotating Detonation Combustor with Dual-Purpose Head-End Injection
item.description: arXiv:2610.30171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rotating detonation engine (RDE) faces severe thermal protection challenges. This study numerically investigates a head-end dual-purpose injection configuration in which the film-cooling holes act as both fuel and coolant injectors. An Eulerian-Lagrangian framework is employed, in which the turbulence closure, the film-cooling effectiveness prediction, and the droplet evaporation model are validated against experimental benchmarks. The validated framework is then applied to examine the effects of coolant flow rate, atomization quality, and the fuel allocation between the main flow and the cooling system. Beyond a threshold coolant flow rate the wall temperature drops substantially, whereas an excessively low flow rate elevates it by intensifying local deflagration, revealing a competition between evaporative cooling and secondary combustion that is inherent to this dual-purpose configuration. Fine droplets cool effectively but only over a limited distance downstream, and fuel allocated to cooling weakens the detonation wave and reduces thrust. A moderate coolant flow rate combined with fine atomization is therefore recommended.
item.dc:creator: Yongbin Zhu, Songbai Yao, Wenwu Zhang

item.title: GeoDiv KAN Solver for Time Fractional Navier Stokes Equations on Complex Domains to Realistic CFD Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2610.30179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientific machine learning provides a promising framework for solving complex problems in science and engineering. Notably, physics informed neural networks (PINNs) have shown considerable potential for solving differential equations and modelling engineering systems. Solving time fractional Navier Stokes equations (TFNSEs) on complex domains is challenging due to temporal nonlocality, nonlinear flow dynamics, geometric complexity, and incompressibility constraints. To address these challenges, we propose a geometry gated, divergence-free Gaussian radial basis function Kolmogorov Arnold network (GeoDiv KAN). The proposed architecture uses geometry dependent feature gating and a streamfunction formulation to preserve incompressibility by construction. GeoDiv KAN is evaluated for the time fractional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on square, circular, and star-shaped domains. Numerical experiments show that GeoDiv KAN achieves higher predictive accuracy than PINN, PIKAN, RBF KAN, and DF RBFKAN across the considered benchmark problems. To establish practical relevance, GeoDiv KAN is applied to two data driven CFD cases: unsteady flow past a circular cylinder using the \href{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5039610}{Zenodo dataset} and turbulent RANS flow through a complex U bend using the \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/JDecke/ubend-cfd}{U-bend dataset}.
item.dc:creator: Yatin Kumar, Shivani Saini, Ramesh Kumar Vats

item.title: Predicting droplet landing in angle-controlled surface acoustic wave jetting
item.description: arXiv:2610.30407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nozzle-free droplet generation eliminates the need for a dispensing orifice, but useful printing also requires control over where droplets are deposited. Here we demonstrate predictable droplet deposition using a nozzle-free, angle-controlled surface acoustic wave jetting platform. Opposing focused interdigital transducers steer droplets from a pendant parent drop toward a collection substrate, with the ejection angle set by the time-integrated acoustic acceleration imbalance. The overall acceleration ratio identifies the operating window for single-droplet ejection and separates it from no-ejection, satellite-droplet, and multiple-droplet regimes. We then connect ejection angle to landing position through a geometric deposition model referenced to a balanced shot in each experiment. At a 5.2 mm parent-drop-to-substrate spacing, 80 steered shots across twenty experiments show strongly anisotropic relative placement scatter: 0.59 mm in the steering direction and 0.06 mm transverse to it. In tests conducted independently over several days, a model calibrated on six earlier collection dates predicted landing positions on two later dates with a root-mean-square error of 0.71 mm; bootstrap resampling placed the 95% confidence range for this error between 0.41 and 1.01 mm. The results establish a practical framework for predicting relative droplet landing in angle-controlled surface acoustic wave jetting and identify the limits imposed by steering angle, separation distance, and actuation regime from an orifice-free, clog-free droplet ejection method.
item.dc:creator: Md Aminul, Sara Adibi, James Friend

item.title: Quartz Crystal Microbalance impedance of discrete adsorbates with lubricated contact
item.description: arXiv:2610.31220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a thorough theoretical investigation of the shear force exerted on a horizontal plate undergoing fast (MHz range) longitudinal oscillations in presence of a spherical particle suspended in the liquid at close proximity to the plate. This hydrodynamic problem is relevant toward the analysis of frequency response (i.e., complex impedance) of Quartz Crystal Microbalance (QCM) to discrete (particulate) adsorbates. For low areal density of adsorbates, the contributions of individual particles remain additive, rendering the theory applicable towards quantitative interpretation of the experimental measurements. For adsorbates much smaller than the viscous penetration depth, the closed-form analytical expressions for the complex impedance were derived for particles of arbitrary density, assuming a lubricated contact (i.e., non-localized adsorption). The theoretical predictions were shown to be in an excellent agreement with accurate Finite Element numerical computations. The validity of the theoretical approach was confirmed by QCM measurements conducted for polystyrene nanoparticles in a broad range of sizes, from 32 nm to 510 nm, adsorbing onto gold/silica sensor upon varying the oscillation frequency.
item.dc:creator: Alexander M. Leshansky, Boris Y. Rubinstein, Marta Sadowska, Zbigniew Adamczyk

item.title: Extracting target-related flow structures using a time-lagged cross-correlation ranking criterion
item.description: arXiv:2610.31245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structures with large global contributions to a flow field are not necessarily those that are most closely associated with a specified engineering observable. We propose a time-lagged cross-correlation (TCC) ranking criterion to extract target-related dynamical structures from a fixed modal expansion while preserving existing spatial modes and temporal coefficients. The criterion ranks mode groups by the mean squared norm of cross-responses between their flow contributions and the observable over a lag window. It is tested separately using dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) and proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). TCC-DMD analysis shows that TCC recovers three low-contribution target structures from a dominant background in a synthetic flow. The reconstruction error for the target subfield is 2.15\%. In the cylinder wake, different force observables select structures associated with the vortex-shedding fundamental, slow drag variations, and the second harmonic. In the cavity case, selected modes connect two main frequency bands of the target observable to distinct spatial amplitude and phase distributions. TCC-POD analysis shows that the criterion minimises the weighted truncation error of the correlation operator among equally sized subsets of the fixed orthogonal basis. A comparison with canonical correlation decomposition further reveals differences between fixed-direction selection and correlation-based basis construction in the spatial structure and retention of flow information. Lag aggregation can improve structure identification when zero-lag association is insufficient. The gains depend on the cross-response distribution and window selection. TCC separates target-related ranking from mode-set construction, enabling comparison of spatial structures associated with different observables within the same modal expansion.
item.dc:creator: Xuran Bao, Zhongkun Jin

item.title: A second-order linear decoupled scheme with a relaxed zero-energy variable for Rayleigh-B\'enard convection
item.description: arXiv:2610.31364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a second-order, linear, and fully decoupled scheme for Rayleigh--B\'enard convection between Navier-slip walls. The nonlinear terms are treated explicitly and multiplied by a scalar with exact value $1$ and no energy contributed to the continuous problem. As a result, each BDF2 step, with a rotational pressure correction, solves only constant-coefficient linear problems. For the time discretization, we prove that, for any time-step, the energy decays when the walls have equal temperatures, under a condition on the thermal weight, and the energy is bounded on finite time intervals when heated from below. Relaxing the scalar towards $1$ preserves both estimates. Energy stability does not control the accuracy of the scalar; the velocity and temperature fields are computed with its unrelaxed value, whose deviation from $1$ scales like $(E/C)(\delta t/\tau)^3$ for kinetic energy $E$, time-scale $\tau$ of the flow, and weight $C$ of the scalar equation. In our tests, choosing $C$ comparable to $E$ keeps this deviation small and doubles the largest time-step for which steady rolls are reproduced to a relative difference of $10^{-8}$. With Taylor--Hood elements, we observe second-order convergence in time, recover the critical Rayleigh numbers, and match published Nusselt numbers to within $0.5\%$. A three-dimensional implementation passes corresponding validation tests.
item.dc:creator: Matthew McCurdy

item.title: Tandem jets in crossflow: the enclosed-recirculation momentum exchange and the unsteady shear-layer dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.31417v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Twin tandem jets in crossflow are examined by 40\ kHz time-resolved particle image velocimetry (PIV) over nine spacing--velocity-ratio conditions ($L=2d$--$4d$, $r\approx3$--7; 68 twin cases, 11 single-jet records). The front jet is diluted: its trajectory lies below the single-jet reference, with a near-field segment up to 40\% shorter, and its velocity ratio falls to an effective value $r_{\mathrm{eff}}<r$, while the shielded rear jet rises above the reference. This paper identifies the carrier of that dilution and the unsteady dynamics that sustains it. The rear-jet blockage closes a gap recirculation whose reversed flow puts the two gap-side layers in the counter-current shear-layer configuration, the classical route to enhanced entrainment. The measured Reynolds stress and Prandtl mixing length show that the absolute exchange is nearly independent of the velocity ratio and exceeds the single-jet leeward zone like-for-like by up to $1.5\times$ (zone peak, across conditions) and $2.8\times$ (area-integrated) at $r\approx7$. The gain comes from an enlarged mixing scale rather than from a steeper shear, and the front-jet near-field shortening follows the absolute exchange transport rather than the twin/single enhancement ratio. The turbulent term exceeds the pressure term in eight of the nine conditions, and the flux budget reads the dilution as a limited mass addition plus a momentum loss to the crossflow; the evidence remains observational. The gap-side layers remain convectively unstable---DMD and SPOD find no growing mode within the resolvable band and record length---so the exchange is carried by convecting vortex trains rather than by a self-excited global mode.
item.dc:creator: Xunchen Liu

item.title: A novel machine learning framework based on proper orthogonal decomposition for turbine wake flow predictions in natural waterways
item.description: arXiv:2610.31547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We developed a machine learning (ML) surrogate trained on instantaneous large eddy simulation (LES) data filtered using proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) to predict mean flow fields in natural rivers with complex geometries. The surrogate enables efficient prediction of mean flow fields downstream of marine hydrokinetic (MHK) turbine arrays at a fraction of the computational cost of high fidelity simulations, facilitating turbine layout optimization in natural waterways where bathymetry, turbulence, and turbine interactions influence the available energy resource. We demonstrate the capabilities of the model at a real world tidal river site under ebb tide conditions. Complex bed bathymetry and planform geometry generate substantial background turbulence that can obscure turbine wake signatures. POD is employed to extract relevant flow structures, improving the ability of the ML model to learn wake dynamics. First, LES is performed at the tidal site to generate training data. POD is then applied to decompose the instantaneous LES fields into spatial modes. Selected modes are used to train a three dimensional convolutional encoder decoder network to predict time averaged velocity fields. This selective filtering reduces the influence of dominant background fluctuations while preserving information relevant to turbine wakes. At equivalent network size and training cost, the POD filtered surrogate reduces the mean squared error by three orders of magnitude compared with the same network trained on unfiltered LES data.
item.dc:creator: Mustafa Meri\c{c} Aksen, Hossein Seyedzadeh, Mehrshad Gholami Anjiraki, Ali Khosronejad

item.title: A Priori Estimation of the Non-Linear Compression Potential and Quantification of Autoencoder Non-Linearity in Turbulent Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.31605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data-driven reduced-order modelling (ROM) of turbulent flows is based on an efficient and physical low-dimensional representation of the flow process. Such a dimension reduction can be achieved using proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) or non-linear autoencoders. Capturing the inherent non-linearities in turbulent flows offers the potential for improved compression rates. This work proposes the local tangent residual (LTR) as an a priori estimate of the potential benefit of non-linear dimension reduction for a given dataset. The LTR is based on the local geometry of the data points, requiring neither prior model training nor the definition of a threshold parameter. For all datasets investigated in this work, namely, two vortex street cases and the turbulent wake flow of a wind turbine, the dominant trends in autoencoder compression performance are reproduced by the proposed LTR. The results are further contextualised through the decoder linearisation error (DLE). The DLE quantifies the non-linearity of the trained decoder by comparing it to a linearised surrogate model, which enables physical interpretability of the non-linearities. Together, a large non-linear compression potential in the turbulent flow, as quantified by the LTR, is corroborated by a large DLE, i.e., a pronounced non-linearity captured in the trained autoencoder. The LTR thus enables practitioners in turbulent flow modelling to determine a priori whether non-linear compression is worthwhile, avoiding the substantial computational cost of autoencoder architecture search and hyperparameter tuning in cases where POD already suffices.
item.dc:creator: Niklas Alexander Pissarski, Juan Pablo Murcia Leon, S{\o}ren Juhl Andersen

item.title: Shear-induced mechanical yielding controls cluster morphology and dynamics in aggregating non-Brownian suspensions
item.description: arXiv:2610.30330v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In sheared aggregating suspensions, flow drives both the formation and breakage of particle clusters, whose dynamic evolution influences transport and rheological properties. Understanding these mechanisms remains challenging due to the complex interplay between interparticle forces, hydrodynamic interactions, and shear flow. Using parallelized Accelerated Stokesian Dynamics (PASD) simulations, we investigate cluster microstructure and rotational dynamics, and how their coupling produces suspension stress in sheared, attractive non-Brownian suspensions. When interparticle attraction dominates over separating shear forces, clusters grow until mechanical loading balances maximum interparticle bond strength. We examine how the cluster stresslet depends on cluster size, with both quantities normalized by their mechanical yielding scales. Scaled cluster stresslets collapse onto a master curve exhibiting three distinct regimes: cubic, quadratic, and linear with respect to the scaled radius of gyration $R_g$. In the cubic regime, small, compact clusters behave as rigid bodies, whose hydrodynamic stresslet scales with cluster volume $R_g^3$. As clusters grow into the quadratic regime, low-aspect-ratio clusters preferentially yield under flow, driving a proportional increase in average aspect ratio with size. High-aspect-ratio clusters follow Jeffery rotational dynamics within the flow-gradient plane, spending longer durations aligned with the flow and thereby reducing their time-averaged hydrodynamic stresslet to scale as $R_g^2$. In the linear regime, clusters approach the maximum size sustainable by the interparticle bonds. The internal tension is bounded by the maximum bond strength, limiting the stresslet to an $R_g$ dependence. These findings establish a mechanistic framework connecting microscale cluster morphology and dynamics to macroscale rheology.
item.dc:creator: Jae Hwan Jeong, Donald L. Koch, Sarah Hormozi

item.title: Finite time implosions of the multidimensional compressible Euler equations with a finite far-field cutoff
item.description: arXiv:2610.30331v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the problem of finite time singularities in the isentropic compressible Euler equations in multiple dimensions with radial symmetry. Our initial data consists of the radially symmetric Kidder self-similar implosion with a continuous constant density cutoff. Motivated by our recent work on the one-dimensional problem, we present high-resolution radially symmetric adaptive mesh refinement simulations that when combined with asymptotic similarity solution analysis present a full picture of the ensuing dynamics of the implosion. From the cutoff point in the initial data, an expanding wave emerges. The endpoints of the wave follow the "imploding" and "exploding" characteristic speeds associated with the system of hyperbolic conservation laws. This wave has much more complex structure than the exact non-centered rarefaction wave that emerges in the one-dimensional problem. As in the one-dimensional case, the inner Kidder solution is swallowed up by the expanding wave as time approaches the singularity time. However, unlike the one-dimensional case, a blowup occurs along the point where the `imploding' side of the expanding wave attaches to the Kidder solution. This composite blowup has an asymptotic self-similar form that has an interpretation in terms of the Gurderley-type self-similarity structure. The numerical method for the PDE necessitates a Lagrangian scheme to avoid the numerical diffusion inherent in Eulerian methods. We use a leapfrog method coupled to recursive refinement of the mesh near the blowup, which allows for very high resolution simulations, resolving many orders of magnitude of the self-similar blowup. Consistent with prior rigorous results for these equations, the blowup does not involve mass concentration and exhibits a critical $L^p$ space for the concentration of the density, depending on the dimension of space.
item.dc:creator: Jack Luong, Reed Spitzer, Scott D. Ramsey, Andrea L. Bertozzi, Roy Baty

item.title: CARS: a centerline-anchored attention surrogate for coronary blood flow on skeleton-generated lumen geometries
item.description: arXiv:2610.30498v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When the parameter of a PDE surrogate is the flow domain itself, the key/value set of an attention model must encode that domain. We present CARS (Coronary Artery Rapid Surrogate), a learned surrogate for the finite-volume solution map of the steady incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on coronary lumens built from image-derived centerlines. CARS maps a centerline with per-point lumen radius and a scalar inlet flow rate to pressure and velocity at arbitrary query points. The attention focal set is the case's own centerline, so geometry fusion costs $O(N n_f)$ rather than $O(N^2)$ in the number of evaluation points. Trained per territory on $2{,}700$ OpenFOAM solutions with synthetic focal lesions, CARS reaches relative $\ell_2$ errors of $0.120/0.149$ (pressure/velocity) on left-coronary and $0.063/0.119$ on right-coronary test sets, in $87$~ms per case against a solver wall-clock of $572$-$1{,}063$~s. It outperforms four parameter-matched neural operators, and accuracy saturates eightfold below the operating focal count. Fractional flow reserve derived from the predicted pressure matches the CFD label at Pearson $r = 0.941/0.993$ and reproduces the $\mathrm{FFR}\le 0.8$ decision in $97.7\%/96.3\%$ of held-out cases. The predicted velocity does not satisfy continuity closely enough for derived quantities, and the weights are territory-specific.
item.dc:creator: Reza Akbarian Bafghi, Sukirt Thakur, Maziar Raissi

item.title: Stiff source terms inside ADER-DG method
item.description: arXiv:2610.30852v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: ADER-DG numerical method with the LST-DG predictor, when used to solve hyperbolic equations with stiff source terms, exhibits properties characteristic of IMEX computational schemes. With increasing stiffness, characterized by the parameter $z = \nu{\Delta t}^{n} < 0$, the maximum of the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}$ of the ADER-DG numerical method increases. In the region of strong stiffness $|z| \gg 1$, a linear increase in the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z) \sim |z|$ occurs. In the region of small source terms $|z| \ll 1$, the results $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z)$ transform into known results for the problem $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(0)$ without source terms. In the transition region $|z| \sim 1$, a range of insignificant decrease in the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z)$ is discovered. In the linear case, instability is violated precisely when one of the matrix eigenvalues reaches $\lambda = -1$, regardless of the phase $\theta$ of the numerical solution. A rigorous stability theory of the ADER-DG numerical method for stiff problems for arbitrary degree $N$ of basis polynomials is constructed. The stability condition is simplified to solving a polynomial equation for the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}$. Highly accurate dependencies of the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(N, z)$ of the ADER-DG method on the parameter $z$ are obtained. A rigorous direct proof of the approximation of the ADER-DG method is presented. Approximation orders $p = N+1$ for arbitrary degrees $N$ are rigorously derived. A set of numerical experiments is carried out to apply the ADER-DG method to solving both a linear advection-reaction equation and the system of Euler equations for a two-component reacting medium. The results obtained in these calculations confirm the theoretical results well.
item.dc:creator: I. S. Popov, A. P. Popova

item.title: Extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method
item.description: arXiv:2610.31072v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Regularized lattice Boltzmann methods improve numerical stability by projecting the nonequilibrium distribution onto its hydrodynamic second-order Hermite sector and filtering the remaining kinetic modes. We introduce a separate relaxation time for the complete complementary kinetic subspace. The resulting extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method (E-RLBM) interpolates continuously between the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook and regularized collision operators while retaining a two-rate implementation. A Chapman-Enskog expansion shows that the isothermal Navier-Stokes equations are recovered with kinematic viscosity $\nu=c_s^2(\tau-\Delta t/2)$, independently of the kinetic relaxation time $\tau_{\rm nh}$, whereas $\tau_{\rm nh}$ changes higher-order truncation errors. For linear transverse shear, its first effect is a fourth-derivative term whose coefficient depends on the direction of propagation relative to the lattice. This fourth-order coefficient is affine in $\tau_{\rm nh}$. For linear shear on D2Q9 and $\tau_{\rm nh}$ between $\tau$ and $\Delta t$, it lies between the corresponding BGK and RLBM values in every propagation direction. Stability maps for the decaying Taylor-Green vortex and flow past a rectangular obstacle show that an appropriate kinetic relaxation substantially enlarges the stable parameter domain. In a Taylor-Green convergence test with consistent initialization, all three operators converge at second order, and their error differences follow the hyperviscous coefficient for diagonal shear waves: the E-RLBM error is about 6% above the BGK error and about 40% below the RLBM error; in a double shear layer at Re = 80000, the E-RLBM follows the RLBM convergence curve. The proposed collision operator therefore provides a low-cost means of controlling nonhydrodynamic modes without introducing a full multiple-relaxation-time basis.
item.dc:creator: Lu\'is Orlando Emerich dos Santos, Diogo Nardelli Siebert

item.title: Anisotropic spin hydrodynamics in a magnetized medium: entropy-current formulation and minimal linear modes
item.description: arXiv:2610.31408v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We formulate anisotropic relativistic spin hydrodynamics in a parity-even magnetized medium using an Israel--Stewart entropy-current construction. Treating the magnetic field at leading order in the gradient expansion reduces the rotational symmetry to $SO(2)$ and separates spin susceptibilities and dissipative transport into longitudinal, transverse, and mixed channels. A restricted quadratic entropy current yields transient equations for the retained dissipative stresses and spin fluxes. We analyze a minimal linear closure around an unpolarized homogeneous equilibrium, retaining dynamical magnetic-flux perturbations but no explicit spin-magnetization coupling; spin and magnetic fluctuations mix through the fluid variables. Infrared coefficient equations and ultraviolet characteristic expansions organize the magnetosonic and Alfv\'en-like spectra together with spectator spin-flux poles. The first-order truncation exhibits unstable boost-sector poles and superlinear large-wave-number branches, interpreted as diagnostics of the truncated equations rather than microscopic dispersion predictions. For the baseline parameters, finite relaxation times yield asymptotically linear propagation branches and finite relaxation poles, with no growing modes found on the sampled grid. The characteristic speeds depend nonmonotonically on spin transport and provide necessary light-cone diagnostics, without establishing general stability or strong hyperbolicity.
item.dc:creator: Yiwei Qiu, Duan She, Defu Hou

item.title: Modulation theory of Y- and X-wave Kadomtsev--Petviashvili solitons
item.description: arXiv:2610.31425v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The evolution of long wavelength perturbations of traveling wave 2-soliton solutions of the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili II (KP) equation are investigated using modulation theory. An initial-boundary value problem for a system of hyperbolic conservation laws is formulated for amplitude and slope perturbations to soliton legs of the resonant (Y-shaped) and X-shaped KP traveling wave solutions. The vertex where individuated soliton legs coalesce is modeled as a moving free boundary where information between the soliton legs can pass. The linearized hyperbolic system is proven to be well-posed under suitable initial conditions and is solved exactly. In the case of the resonant Y-shaped soliton, all admissible simple (rarefaction) waves of the nonlinear system are characterized. Specific perturbations of Y-waves can lead to the dimensionality of the modulated solution changing, corresponding to a physical geometric change to the multi-soliton pattern. Spontaneous leg deletion and leg creation can occur. The conditions under which the Y-wave modulation system can experience gradient catastrophe are given. Gradient catastrophe is regularized by the formation of a new leg, with an augmented modulation system proposed to describe the growth of the new leg. On the other hand, the X-wave system can be reduced to two independent line soliton modulation systems. These findings reinforce the prevalence and generality of resonant Y-shaped vertices in the KP II system and applications.The theoretical modulation predictions are supported by direct numerical simulations of KP II, which show good agreement with the analysis.
item.dc:creator: Jerry Wang, Mark A. Hoefer

item.title: Tandem jets in crossflow: a one-parameter dilution law for the trajectory and the velocity decay
item.description: arXiv:2409.19927v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The front jet of a tandem pair in crossflow is not passive. This paper treats the mean-flow phenomenology and its scaling; the mechanism is left to the companion paper. In 40\ kHz time-resolved PIV measurements covering nine spacing--velocity-ratio conditions ($L=2d$, $3d$, $4d$; $r\approx3$, $5$, $7$) and a single-jet baseline, the front-jet $rd$-normalized trajectory lies below the single-jet reference in every condition (near-field segment up to 40\% shorter), while the shielded rear jet rises above the reference in eight of the nine and penetrates $1.4$--$2.0$ times deeper than the front jet. The mean pressure and reverse-flow statistics are inconsistent with the two classical explanations: the inter-jet region is pressurized rather than sub-atmospheric, the lateral pressure difference across the front jet is weakened rather than enhanced (within reconstruction uncertainty), and the reverse-flow region does not follow the ordering of the modification. In natural coordinates the centerline decay re-scales onto the single-jet law at the effective velocity ratio (seven of nine within 18\%), so bending and decay are two readouts of one dilution, which whole-trajectory matching condenses into the one-parameter law $r_{\mathrm{eff}}/r=r/(r+c)$, $c=3.31$, with the velocity ratio as the primary control and the spacing entering through the near-field capacity ($c_h=2.50$--$3.30$). The law has one fitted constant and needs only the single-jet reference family; leave-one-condition-out predictions reproduce each held-out condition within 15\%, so the procedure is portable to any tandem array in which the gap recirculation closes.
item.dc:creator: Xunchen Liu

item.title: On buoyancy in disperse two-phase flow and its impact on the well-posedness of two-fluid models
item.description: arXiv:2507.21602v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Maxey--Riley--Gatignol equation for the flow around a sphere at low particle Reynolds number tells us that the fluid-particle interaction force decomposes into a contribution from the local flow disturbance caused by the particle's boundary---consisting of the drag, virtual-mass, and history forces, and their Fax\'en corrections---and another contribution from the stress of the background flow, termed generalized-buoyancy force. There is also a consensus that, for general disperse two-phase flow, the interfacial force density, coupling the average fluid phase and dispersed-phase momentum balances, decomposes in a like manner. However, there has been a long-standing controversy about the physical closure separating the generalized-buoyancy from the interfacial force density, especially whether or not pseudo-stresses, such as the Reynolds stress, should be attributed to the background flow. Furthermore, most existing propositions for this closure involve small-particle approximations. Here, we show that all existing buoyancy closures are inconsistent with particle-resolving numerical simulations and/or at least one of two simple thought experiments designed to determine the roles of pseudo-stresses and small-particle approximations. We then derive the unique consistent closure. It requires no approximation and implies that all stresses and pseudo-stresses in the average fluid phase momentum balance, except the Reynolds stress, fully contribute to the background flow responsible for buoyancy. Remarkably, it exhibits a low-pass filter property, attenuating buoyancy at short wavelengths, that prevents it from causing Hadamard instabilities, constituting a first-principles-based solution to the long-standing ill-posedness problem of two-fluid models. When employing the derived closure, even simplistic two-fluid models are linearly well-posed.
item.dc:creator: Rui Zhu, Yulan Chen, Katharina Tholen, Zhiguo He, Thomas P\"ahtz

item.title: Global non-equilibrium thermodynamics of stationary states applied to the Rayleigh-B\'enard convection
item.description: arXiv:2510.05389v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Classical thermodynamics describes physical systems in thermodynamic equilibrium, characterized in particular by the absence of macroscopic motion. Global non-equilibrium thermodynamics extends this framework to include physical systems in stationary states (Ho{\l}yst et al., EPL 149, 30001 (2025)). Here, we demonstrate that this extended theory captures macroscopic motion in stationary states, thereby providing a unified framework for global thermodynamics and fluid mechanics. We apply the theory to stationary Rayleigh-B\'enard convection and show how the second law of global non-equilibrium thermodynamics determines the direction of changes in fluid motion.
item.dc:creator: Robert Ho{\l}yst, Pawe{\l} Jan \.Zuk, Konrad Gi\.zy\'nski, Anna Macio{\l}ek, Jakub Wr\'obel, Peter Vaughan Elsmere McClintock

item.title: Nonhomogeneous elastic turbulence in the two-dimensional Taylor-Couette flow
item.description: arXiv:2510.13475v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Elastic turbulence is a spatially and temporally disordered flow state appearing in viscoelastic fluids at vanishing fluid inertia and large elasticity. The resulting flows have broad technological interest, particularly to enhance mixing and heat transfer in microdevices. Although its experimental characterization is now well established in different setups, its theoretical understanding and numerical reproducibility remain challenging, especially in wall-bounded geometries. By means of numerical simulations, we investigate the onset of elastic turbulence and the characteristics of the developed turbulent-like states in the two-dimensional, confined, Taylor-Couette system. First, we characterize the purely elastic instability, addressing previously contrasting evidences. We then show that the fully nonlinear dynamics are weakly anisotropic and strongly nonhomogeneous. Indeed, they are confined in a dynamically active region adjacent to the inner wall, akin to the elastic boundary layer from previous predictions. Within this region,in spite of some non-negligible deviations due to the nonhomeogeneity of our setup, the statistical and spectral turbulent properties are to reasonable extent not far from the theoretical expectations and experimental observations.
item.dc:creator: Zhongxuan Hou, Stefano Berti, Teodor Burghelea, Francesco Roman\`o

item.title: Perspiration vapor lightens near skin air but hinders human evaporative cooling in arid heat
item.description: arXiv:2511.16922v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sweat evaporation is the body's primary cooling mechanism, yet the physical factors governing it are not fully understood. We identify a dueling buoyancy effect in the context of the human body, in which perspiration vapor reduces the near skin air density, counteracting the downward flow driven by cooling of warm air upon contact with the skin. In hot, arid, stagnant environments, this opposing buoyancy suppresses free convection and can reduce sweat evaporation by more than half. As a result, commonly used thermoregulation models can substantially underpredict body temperature (e.g., by 1C after 2 hours of exposure to typical Arizona summer conditions). We develop compact, physics informed models for free convective heat transfer coefficients across wide temperature and humidity ranges, enabling improved thermoregulation modeling and thermal audits. These results enhance understanding of human heat balance and support more accurate heat stress assessment to inform behavioral, infrastructural, and policy decisions for extreme heat adaptations.

item.title: Long-time turbulence prediction at fine time steps using multi-stride neural operators
item.description: arXiv:2604.12794v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-time turbulence prediction at fine time steps is costly and prone to error accumulation, while accurate short-term fields do not ensure accurate long-time statistics. We propose a multi-stride neural operator for three-dimensional turbulence, combining implicit factorized Transformer (IFF) predictors with a factorized-attention cross-stride fusion (FA-CSF) module. All predictors take the same current velocity field as input. FA-CSF reuses their outputs and latent features to generate intermediate velocity fields through interpolation and learned correction. The corrected largest-stride field drives the next autoregressive step, decoupling the autoregressive step from the output time step. Stride-conditioned IFF (SC-IFF) predictors are first trained at power-of-two strides using three conditioning strategies, then frozen while FA-CSF is trained on long rollouts with field-data and statistical losses. Tests on turbulent channel flow and forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) show improved long-time predictions and statistics. At a sampling interval of 10 direct numerical simulation (DNS) time steps, fixed-stride IFF yields relative L2 errors above 100% in channel-flow root-mean-square (RMS) velocity fluctuation profiles and the Reynolds shear stress profile, and in the temporal evolution of velocity and vorticity RMS values and the time-averaged energy spectrum in HIT. SC-IFF with independent stride-specific predictors and FA-CSF keeps statistics close to filtered DNS data over the tested prediction times. Relative to fixed-stride IFF, it reduces errors in the channel-flow profiles by more than 98% and in the HIT spectrum by more than 99%. Multi-stride prediction with FA-CSF generates trajectories at fine time steps 3.69 times faster than fixed-stride IFF autoregression and 2.41 times faster than hierarchical multi-stride prediction.
item.dc:creator: Guanyu Pan, Huiyu Yang, Yunpeng Wang, Zikun Xu, Nianyu Yi, Jianchun Wang

item.title: A Particle Multi-Relaxation Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook Method for Rarefied Monatomic Gas Mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2604.24244v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Kinetic models based on the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) framework provide an efficient alternative to the Boltzmann equation for rarefied gas flows; however, existing formulations for gas mixtures remain limited in representing pair-dependent relaxation processes and recovering correct Navier-Stokes-Fourier (NSF) transport behavior. A particle-based unified BGK (UBGK) model for monatomic gas mixtures is developed by extending the single-species UBGK framework to a multi-relaxation formulation. The model preserves the pairwise interaction structure of the mixture Boltzmann equation, enabling independent species-pair relaxations for an arbitrary number of species. The relaxation properties of the mixture UBGK model are determined by matching the production terms to those of the Boltzmann equation, ensuring correct NSF-level transport behavior. The model is implemented within the particle framework and validated against DSMC using four benchmark cases: homogeneous relaxation, Poiseuille flow, Couette flow, and hypersonic flow around a cylinder. The results demonstrate that the mixture UBGK model captures species-specific non-equilibrium effects, including species-dependent differences in velocity and temperature, across a range of mole fractions and Knudsen numbers in good agreement with DSMC. Furthermore, cost and accuracy analyses show that the mixture UBGK model becomes more efficient than DSMC at sufficiently large time step sizes, but its first-order accuracy suggests further improvement through higher-order schemes.
item.dc:creator: Inchan Kim, Joonbeom Kim, Woonghwi Park, Eunji Jun

item.title: Linear causality and stability constraints on relativistic second-order magnetohydrodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2606.00649v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we construct a theoretical framework for relativistic second-order magnetohydrodynamics based on entropy current analysis. The formalism consistently incorporates finite relaxation dynamics of the dissipative fluxes, providing a transient framework suitable for analyzing linear stability and short-wavelength causality. Utilizing linear mode analysis, we investigate the constraints imposed by causality and stability on this anisotropic system. By linearizing the theory around a homogeneous equilibrium state, we identify the magnetosonic, Alfv\'en, and charge-diffusion sectors, together with their coupling terms. For each sector, we derive asymptotic dispersion relations in both the long-wavelength (small-$k$) and short-wavelength (large-$k$) regimes, validating them against exact numerical roots. Our numerical analysis confirms the accuracy of these asymptotic solutions and uncovers a nontrivial angular dependence, especially near special propagation directions where the ordinary momentum expansion becomes less reliable. By evaluating the large-$k$ behavior of the propagating branches alongside the damping properties of non-hydrodynamic modes, we delineate the corresponding causality constraints. We find that the admissible linear causal domain is governed by the interplay between propagation direction, anisotropic transport coefficients, and relaxation times, with the resulting bounds being intrinsically mode-dependent. These findings provide a systematic theoretical basis for investigating linear stability and short-wavelength causality in relativistic magnetohydrodynamics beyond the first-order approximation.
item.dc:creator: Yiwei Qiu, Duan She, Defu Hou

item.title: Directional Control of Droplet Motion via Geometric Gating
item.description: arXiv:2609.38654v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We explore new methods for inducing the movement of water droplets on elastomeric substrates, such as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). Our approach builds upon the well-known phenomenon that water droplets move easily across these substrates when swelled w,ith silicone oil. While designing shallow open channels and traps on a PDMS film offers a simple way to control a droplet's trajectory by tilting the substrate in two orthogonal directions, this method is poorly suited for manipulating multiple droplets simultaneously. To address this limitation, we introduce two new methods. The first method utilizes a plano-concave PDMS platform with a radius of curvature significantly larger than the size of the droplet and its translation distance. When the system's configuration is altered, this curved substrate consistently guides the droplet along a curved geodesic. The second method incorporates diode-like gates on the PDMS. These gates are created on either flat or plano-concave PDMS films by embedding thin, rigid plates into the elastomer prior to crosslinking, followed by swelling in silicone oil. This process generates sigmoidal steps that restrict droplet motion to a single direction. Finally, we demonstrate how combining these two strategies enables various forms of directed motion for both single and multiple droplets.
item.dc:creator: Manoj K. Chaudhury, Vanessa Elias, Michelle Fruge
